extracted.intended_audience: scholars and practitioners studying administrative rulemaking, notice-and-comment participation, and public administration (e.g., political scientists, legal scholars, agency staff, policy analysts)
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluating how administrative agencies respond to mass comment campaigns in rulemaking, comparing procedural referencing and substantive outcomes for campaign comments versus non-campaign comments. Uses empirical analysis of EPA rulemakings (2012–2017).

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural referencing of mass comment campaigns
rubrics_metrics.description: Procedurally, the agency references mass comment campaigns in its responses to comments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article finds that agencies do make procedural references to mass comment campaigns when responding, indicating acknowledgement at the response stage; this is an observable procedural measure of responsiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Citation rate of campaigns vs other comments
rubrics_metrics.description: The agency cites campaigns at lower rates than other comments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comparative citation frequency (how often a comment or campaign is explicitly cited in the agency's response) is used as an indicator of attention; lower citation rates for campaigns suggest reduced procedural engagement relative to individually unique comments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Outcome consistency between regulations and requested changes
rubrics_metrics.description: The agency's regulations are generally not consistent with changes requested in comments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluates substantive effect of comments on final regulatory text or policy decisions — whether requested changes are adopted. The article reports a general lack of association between comments and regulatory change, used as a substantive responsiveness metric.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differential outcome association for mass campaigns
rubrics_metrics.description: A lack of association between comments and regulatory changes holds especially for mass comment campaigns (i.e., campaigns are less associated with policy changes than other comments).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When comparing campaign comments to non-campaign comments, mass campaigns demonstrate especially weak associations with desired regulatory outcomes, implying diminished substantive influence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presence of 'relevant matter' in comments
rubrics_metrics.description: Mass comment campaigns — relative to other comments — generally contain little 'relevant matter.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Content quality metric: comments containing substantive, case-specific, or technically relevant information ('relevant matter') are more likely to affect agency responsiveness. Mass campaigns often lack such content, which helps explain lower influence or citation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal imperatives versus political considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Legal imperatives trump political considerations in conditioning agency responsiveness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpretive standard: agencies prioritize legal and technical constraints over political signals from mass comment counts. This implies that criteria tied to legal relevance and statutory/administrative requirements matter more for responsiveness than volume of similar comments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparative responsiveness metric (campaigns vs non-campaign comments)
rubrics_metrics.description: Assessment of responsiveness compares comments submitted as part of mass campaigns to comments submitted outside of campaigns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The study's central comparative dimension: responsiveness should be evaluated along both procedural (references/citations) and outcome (adoption of requested changes) axes, comparing campaign and non-campaign comment sets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical scope as an evaluation constraint
rubrics_metrics.description: Analysis focuses on 1,049 mass comment campaigns that occurred during 22 EPA rulemakings between 2012 and 2017.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When applying findings or evaluating similar phenomena, consider this temporal, institutional, and sample scope — results may depend on agency (EPA), time period (2012–2017), and the operational definition of 'mass comment campaign.'
